source.title: Scaling-Aware Data Selection for End-to-End Autonomous Driving Systems
source.authors: Tolga Dimlioglu; Nadine Chang; Ma-Ying Shen; Rafid Mahmood; José M. Álvarez

record.file_problem: Full paper and supplementary material are present. Some figure text and formatting are imperfectly extracted, but the main text and relevant tables are readable.
record.tranche_reason: Applies scaling-based data selection to end-to-end autonomous driving and reports how driving metrics vary with added data, a new task and training setting relative to language-model loss scaling.
record.gate_note: The paper cites language-model scaling laws but does not test language-model held-out cross-entropy, parameter-count scaling, training-compute scaling, or a compute-optimal parameter/token split. Its own scaling results concern EPDMS versus added driving clips and use a saturating exponential. Rows below cover those reported scaling results; baseline comparisons between data-selection methods are omitted because they do not themselves test the scaling-law claims.
record.test_reason: The study uses scaling fits as a tool inside the MOSAIC data-selection method. It assumes a saturating exponential (not a power law) for EPDMS gain versus clips added per domain, fitted on two continual fine-tuning pilot runs, and reports mainly the method's EPDMS and BRMR against baselines. It never tests language-model loss scaling, compute-optimal allocation, architecture shape, or whether a power-law form holds in driving. Table 5 checks the additive cluster approximation of the authors' own tool, not a scaling-law claim.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also claim the cross-cluster interaction terms are 'present but negligible' (overestimate 'up to 1 EPMS'), even though Table 5 shows a 1.5-point gap at 800 clips. They frame Table 5 as an upper bound on interactions because it also includes extrapolation error. They also claim MOSAIC's pilot-run compute amortises at large budgets.
record.recipe_differences: The study applies a data-selection method for autonomous-driving metrics, fitting a saturating exponential to utility improvement as samples are added. It does not reproduce language-model loss scaling or compute-optimal training allocation.
record.method_sensitivity: Cluster domains have different fitted gains and saturation behavior. The authors report that the approximation can be less suitable when clusters lack semantic coherence; caption-based clustering also changes baseline performance, particularly for Chameleon.

fits_no_version.finding: For a fixed Hydra-MDP planner, per-domain gains in the driving score EPDMS are modelled with a saturating exponential a(1-e^{-n/τ}). Each curve is fitted from two continual fine-tuning pilot runs. Summing the cluster fits overestimates actual Navtrain EPDMS by 0.5 to 1.5 points at 200–2400 clips and underestimates it by 0.1 at 100 clips.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Data-scaling of a driving planner's metric per data domain follows a saturating curve that is predictable from small pilot runs.

record.problems: The scaling validation shown in Table 5 is for Navtrain and estimates overstate actual EPDMS at several larger budgets. The authors state that discrepancies combine cross-cluster interactions and extrapolation error, so interaction error is not isolated. The experiments use one planner model and two data settings; the reported fits are for added samples, not language-model loss or model/compute scaling.
record.rows_left_out: No separate rows for the extensive EPDMS/BRMR comparisons among selection strategies: those are outcomes of the data-selection methods rather than direct measurements of the claim’s scaling relationships. Figure-only numeric curve readings are not transcribed.

untested.parts: All: no LM held-out loss vs parameters, tokens or compute.
All: no extrapolation of LM loss. Only two-point saturating fits on driving data are used as a tool.
No test of whether a power law holds in driving. A saturating exponential is assumed, and no functional forms are compared.
No downstream performance versus model scale or pretraining loss. A single planner model is used throughout.
No comparison of fitting choices or exponents.

record.verdict_notes: This is a data-selection methods paper, so it is T4. It cites Kaplan et al. only as motivation. The functional form is assumed rather than tested, and the fits come from just two pilot points per cluster using short continual training. All of the record's V5/V6 links and labels should be dropped.

versions.untested_parts: Language-model held-out loss versus parameter count, tokens, or compute.
Extrapolating language-model loss from small runs to much larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocation, and how either scales with compute.
Effects of language-model depth, width, and other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.

The study tests scaling of driving evaluation metrics against added data in autonomous driving, but does not test language-model power laws or other listed modalities and regimes. It uses a saturating exponential rather than comparing power-law fits.
The study examines predictability of an autonomous-driving evaluation metric from added data, not language-model downstream performance versus model scale or pretraining loss.
Language-model exponent and compute-optimal-split sensitivity to parameter counting, schedule, data, or fitting choices.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Autonomous-driving EPDMS as a function of added clips
reader_labels.reason: The study reports cluster-specific scaling in this new setting but models it with a saturating exponential, not a demonstrated common power-law form; the fit comparisons in r1–r10 do not establish that the language-model power law transfers unchanged.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Navtrain EPDMS estimated from cluster-wise fits at the reported clip budgets
reader_labels.reason: Estimated EPDMS tracks actual EPDMS closely at the reported budgets, though estimates are higher by 0.5 to 1.5 points at several larger budgets (r1–r6).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: OpenScene EPDMS by domain and amount of added data
reader_labels.reason: The study reports differing, fitted improvement trends by data domain, including gains that diminish with added clips and a domain that becomes more favorable at higher budgets (r7–r10).
